title: Measurement of hydrogen peroxide vapor in powders with potassium titanium oxide oxalate loaded cellulose pellets as probes
author: Kastvig, Bøtker, et al.

steps.title: Prepare potassium titanium oxide oxalate solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve potassium titanium oxide oxalate (PTO) powder in Milli‑Q water to obtain a solution concentration between 0.001 M and 0.100 M, then adjust the solution to pH 3.0 using 3.0 M HCl solution.

substeps.instruction: Weigh the desired amount of PTO powder.
Add Milli‑Q water and stir until fully dissolved.
Measure pH and add 3.0 M HCl dropwise until pH 3.0 is reached.

steps.title: Load PTO onto cellulose pellets
steps.instruction: In a Blue‑Cap flask, combine 0.0354 g to 3.541 g PTO powder with 100 mL Milli‑Q water, adjust the mixture to pH 3.0 with 3.0 M HCl, then transfer the resulting PTO solution to a round‑bottom flask containing 20.0 g cellulose pellets (Cellet®); use a flask of at least 0.5 L to provide sufficient surface area.

substeps.instruction: Add PTO powder to 100 mL Milli‑Q water in a Blue‑Cap flask.
Adjust pH to 3.0 with 3.0 M HCl.
Place 20.0 g cellulose pellets in a round‑bottom flask (≥0.5 L).
Pour the PTO solution onto the pellets and mix gently.

steps.title: Dry PTO‑loaded pellets
steps.instruction: Dry the pellet mixture on a Büchi Rotavapor R‑144 equipped with a Büchi B‑480 water bath at 60–65 °C, 80–130 mbar pressure, and approximately 50 rpm rotation for about 1 hour, ensuring rotation is not slower to avoid pellet aggregation.

steps.title: Confirm complete drying and post‑dry treatment
steps.instruction: Weigh the flask to verify that all water has evaporated; if excess water is detected, place the pellet sample in a heating cabinet at 60 °C overnight and re‑weigh until the mass is stable.

substeps.instruction: If weight indicates residual water, transfer pellets to a heating cabinet at 60 °C.
Leave overnight, then re‑weigh to confirm complete drying.

steps.title: Measure water activity (optional)
steps.instruction: Determine the water activity of the dried PTO‑loaded pellets using an Aqualab 3 TE instrument.

steps.title: Test for PTO dust transfer (optional)
steps.instruction: Add one drop of 30 % hydrogen peroxide to the water in the Rotavapor receiver and observe that no yellow color forms, confirming that no PTO dust was transferred.

steps.title: Store PTO pellets
steps.instruction: Store the dried PTO‑loaded pellets in a refrigerator at 5–10 °C; they remain stable for at least 6 months under these conditions.

description: Hydrogen peroxide vapor can cause stability problems of active ingredients in dry granular mixes such as powder detergents with added bleach particles [2], [3], [4], [5]. The aim of this study was to develop an experimental method to quantify the amount of H2O2 vapor inside powders at an interparticle level. Xu et al. showed that hydrogen peroxide vapor pressures could be measured by reflectance measurements of color changes of adsorbed titanyl salts absorbed into dry paper tissues [1]. Titanyl salts react with hydrogen peroxide and form yellow-colored epoxides (Fig. 1) [6]. We here report a method based on cellulose particles loaded with titanyl salt to measure H2O2 vapor in powder systems. Cellulose pellets are available commercially as Cellet®, which are microcrystalline cellulose particles. They are spherical and have open porous structures and come with diameters ranging from 100 to 1400 µm, which makes them useful as probes in many powder systems, as they can be chosen to have sizes that are within the particle size distribution of such systems. We have used the method to measure hydrogen peroxide vapor in bleach-containing detergent powder in order to estimate shelf life stability of the detergent powder in different storage conditions [7]. Cellulose pellets are not water soluble, but efficiently ad/absorb water and water soluble compounds [8].Fig. 1Reaction between potassium titanium oxide oxalate, PTO, and hydrogen peroxide.Fig. 1 In this work cellulose pellets were loaded with potassium titanium oxide oxalate (PTO), and the hydrogen peroxide induced color change of these PTO loaded pellets were tested as probe particles in dry systems. Xu et al. [1] developed a method based on ammonium titanyl oxalate (ATO) adsorbed into paper tissue to measure hydrogen peroxide vapor pressures.
